episodes.title: The Kibwetere Story | LazyPod Ep. 4
episodes.description:
On 17 March 2000, Uganda witnessed one of the deadliest cult-related tragedies in modern history. At the centre of the tragedy was the Movement for the Restoration of the Ten Commandments of God, a doomsday religious movement led by Joseph Kibwetere, Credonia Mwerinde and Catholic priest Dominic Kataribabo, among others. The group emerged in the late 1980s after its leaders claimed to receive divine visions and warnings about the approaching end of the world.

As the year 2000 approached, followers were reportedly encouraged to sell their possessions and prepare for an expected journey to heaven. When the predicted apocalypse did not occur, tensions grew within the movement. Members began questioning the leadership and, according to investigators, some demanded their property back.

On 17 March 2000, hundreds of followers gathered inside the group's church at Kanungu in southwestern Uganda. The building was set on fire, killing hundreds. Initially, the incident was widely described as a mass suicide, but the discovery of additional bodies in mass graves and other locations changed the investigation. Authorities increasingly treated the wider tragedy as a mass murder orchestrated by the group's leadership.

One of the most disturbing discoveries was made at property associated with Dominic Kataribabo, where investigators found dozens of bodies. Kataribabo himself was among the cult leaders believed to have died in the Kanungu fire. Meanwhile, Joseph Kibwetere and Credonia Mwerinde disappeared and were never conclusively accounted for, leading to years of speculation about whether they escaped.

The Kanungu massacre remains a devastating example of how charismatic authority, apocalyptic beliefs and the isolation of followers can combine with deadly consequences. More than two decades later, the tragedy continues to raise difficult questions about how the movement operated, why warnings were not acted upon earlier, and what ultimately happened to its missing leaders.
